Two findings that changed the framing:

1. The ERROR path is checker-driven too, not just the inference path. Only 5 of the 20 TS9xxx diagnostics are raised under an isolatedDeclarations guard in transform.go; the other 15 -- including TS9007/9010/9011/9012 -- come from tracker.go:92, inside the SymbolTracker the checker's node builder calls when it fails. Upstream answers 'does this need inference?' by running the inference and watching it fail. There is no syntactic predicate to port. This makes option (a) even less viable than this issue assumed.

The .d.ts OUTPUT oracle really is 6 cases, but 16 cases carry TS9xxx diagnostics in their .errors.txt baselines -- 20 distinct codes, ~172 positioned diagnostics -- and those measure exactly the checker-free half, with positions and codes. Fixed. The rule was narrower than the issue assumed: TS9009 fires only for a LONE accessor -- a get/set pair is never reported even when neither half is annotated (isolatedDeclarationErrorsClasses puts all four combinations side by side and only getOnly/setOnly are squiggled). A setter anchors at its PARAMETER, not its name. One asymmetry taken from the baselines rather than derived: a lone unannotated getter reports in a class and is silent in an object literal. Also fixed the real cause of the neighbouring TS9038 gap -- class accessors never had their computed names checked at all, and TS9038 suppresses TS9009 at the same position.

Fixed, and the predicate was wrong in a more interesting way than 'too eager'. TS9020 is three-valued, not boolean: a call initializer (A = computed(0)) is NOT an error, because a non-constant expression emits as a computed member with no value at all. Only a constant-SHAPED expression that reaches outside the enum errors. And it is transitive -- enum F { A = E.A, B = A } reports twice, because B names a sibling that is itself not constant -- so members are folded in declaration order, each seeing the verdicts before it. Self-references by any spelling (A, Flag.AB, Flag["A"]) stay inside. Anchored at the member name, not the initializer. 0/7 -> 7/7.

Fixed, and the answer was the opposite of what this issue proposed. A computed name must be WRITTEN as a literal -- not merely have a literal type. isolatedDeclarationErrorsObjects puts six computed names in one object literal and accepts only [1]: [s] where const s: unique symbol, [E.V] where E is an enum, and [k] where const k = 'a' are ALL reported. Classes agree. So the syntactic rule is not an approximation of upstream here, it is exact: literal, optionally signed ([-1] ok, [1-1] not).

A scope index resolving names to literal-typed consts was built and removed twice -- the second attempt aimed at interface I's [noAnnotationLiteralName](), which turned out not to be a computed-name rule at all: that member is missing a RETURN TYPE, and upstream pairs its TS9013 with TS7010.

Partly fixed, partly established as out of reach -- which was the question this issue asked.

Implemented: TS9021 (extends clause that is not an entity name), TS9022 in the remaining position, TS9019 (binding element with an initializer -- fires even when the declaration IS annotated), TS9013 on interface method signatures, and the 6 false-positive TS9007 in ReturnTypes (an arrow with a concise LITERAL body needs no return type; only block bodies do).

NOT implementable syntactically, established rather than assumed:
- TS9025 (implicitly adding undefined). Upstream uses EmitResolver.RequiresAddingImplicitUndefined. The corpus gives one discriminating pair: foo(p = (ip = 10, ...)) is clean, foo2(p = (ip = 10 as T, ...)) with type T = number is reported. The difference is the initializer's TYPE, not its shape. tsr-49v.1's audit flagged this as the item most likely to resist; it does. Phase 4.
- TS9026 (preserving an import for augmentations). Needs to know that ANOTHER file contains declare module './parent'. That is Program-level, not checker-level, so it is reachable before Phase 4 but not from analyze(file, nodes).

Built: crates/tsr-conformance/src/js_baseline.rs, the //// [name] section splitter, validated corpus-wide by an independent count rather than only by unit tests.

Three things the format does that a naive splitter gets wrong, each confirmed across all 11,714 .js baselines in compiler/ and conformance/:

1. The first line is a section-looking line that is NOT a section -- it names the case, and is distinguished only by a trailing '////'. Zero other lines in the corpus carry that shape, so the discriminator is sound rather than a guess.
2. Section names REPEAT. An @allowJs case echoes file.js as source and then emits file.js again; both are real and differ. The reader keeps an ordered Vec, never a map -- a map would drop one of every such pair, always the input, in exactly the cases where JS input is what is under test.
3. [DtsFileErrors] is not a file. 22 baselines carry it; its body is an errors.txt-shaped block of diagnostics the GENERATED .d.ts produces. Exposed separately from the file sections.

Also: declaration sections are .d.ts, .d.mts AND .d.cts. Matching .d.ts alone misses 495 sections (247 mts + 248 cts) and would report every ESM/CJS declaration case as emitting nothing.

Done, but NOT as ADR-0029 specified — the guard policy was implemented, falsified, and replaced.

WHAT WAS BUILT FIRST (ADR-0029 step 2): MAX_DEPTH=1000 guards in tsr-binder's bind() and tsr-printer's expression dispatch, a project-specific diagnostic (code 900000, outside upstream's space), and an iterative left-spine emit for binary chains. All suites held. WORKER_STACK came down 32 MiB -> 8 MiB.

WHY THAT WAS NOT ENOUGH: at 8 MiB the conformance run still aborted, in printer_round_trip, on a THIRD unguarded recursive walk — tsr_ast::visit::walk_node, the generated generic visitor. It is not harness code: it is the public walk every consumer uses, including the checker to come. A depth guard fits it badly because Visit is a trait with user-written impls and the counter has nowhere to live.

Generalised: a guard policy needs every recursive walk to opt in and is silently wrong until the last one does. That is ADR-0028's 'pushes the problem onto every caller' objection, theoretical then and measured now.

DECIDED BY OWNER, implemented: grow the stack natively (stacker via tsr_core::stack::ensure_sufficient, rustc's constants), accept that wasm32 traps. ADR-0030 supersedes ADR-0029. The guards and the invented diagnostic were removed; the printer's spine flattening was kept as a pure win (byte-identical output).

MEASURED. bind depth over 16,207 corpus files (new examples/bind_depth.rs): p50 7, p90 11, p99 16, p99.9 25, deepest non-chain 285, deepest overall 4,958 (binderBinaryExpressionStress, 2 files). stack_depth parse+bind at depth 5,000 collapsed to the parse column: binary 4M->1M, parens 8M->1M, arraytype 4M->1M. WORKER_STACK now 8 MiB and the suite is green there.
